nodes.label: Swarm Ledger (candidate S4A)
nodes.rationale: Log-only, self-hostable, append-only per-operator record with a stable swarm_id across runs, plus an exported ruleset that targets the cluster rather than the user-agent. SURVIVING WEDGE with a tarpit risk on one input (log fields) and a serious prior-art hit on the mechanism claim: the insight line 'nobody answers whether these 9,000 requests are one actor' is falsifiable in one search and must be rewritten.

nodes.label: Operator-owned artifacts: ledger, evidence rows, case card, ruleset export
nodes.rationale: Where the wedge actually lives: the segment (self-hosted/small operators, validated by Logrip's 80-95% figure), the artifacts (ledger + evidence rows + case card + cluster-targeting ruleset export, which none of the four opened products produces for the operator), persistence-as-a-feature ('the same swarm is back and it is now using 40 ASNs' is a diff across runs), and ownership (your ledger, your logs, no vendor in the path).

nodes.label: Spoof-resistant join key set (JA4, HTTP/2 SETTINGS, header order, Web Bot Auth keyid, ASN//24, path shingles, timing lockstep)
nodes.rationale: TARPIT RISK, and it is about data rather than rivals: JA4, HTTP/2 SETTINGS and header order are not in a default nginx/Apache access log and are absent from every public log release found, so they cannot be obtained retroactively. The keys already present in every log are ASN//24 (needs raw IP), path-sequence shingles and timing lockstep. The money line 'they spoofed their user-agent but the JA4 matched' cannot be shown on public real data.

nodes.label: WebDecoy
nodes.source_location: startup — CLOSEST COMMERCIAL MATCH ON MECHANISM
nodes.rationale: Closest commercial match on mechanism — 'WebDecoy uses JA4 as a correlation key inside a persistent actor identity' and 'fingerprints identify software. Actors identify attackers'. Wedge: it is an inline bot-detection-and-mitigation platform that must sit in front of your traffic, discloses no pricing and no self-host/log-only path, does not specify cross-day persistence, and produces no append-only ledger, per-cluster evidence rows, case card, exported robots.txt/nginx map/CDN expression or cross-run swarm diff. A blocking service, not an operator-owned record.

nodes.label: DataDome
nodes.rationale: PARTLY: aggregates signals across request, session, IP and fingerprint over different time windows and documents the same URL fetched by bots with the same signature from 10+ IPs in one minute. But no evidence of a durable, customer-queryable per-operator entity with a stable id across days — attribution happens inside the engine to decide block/allow, and the customer receives classification plus analytics. Window-scoped (minutes) vs cross-run persistence (days/weeks); no operator-facing ledger or cluster-targeting ruleset export.

nodes.label: Netacea
nodes.rationale: PARTLY: closest commercial claim to 'the same actor is back' — a proprietary User ID assigning an identity to each visitor without PII, plus attacker fingerprints combined from across the Netacea customer network. But the identity is per-visitor plus vendor-side cross-customer threat intel, not a per-operator cluster record the operator owns; server-side log ingestion exists only as a customer; no self-host and no cluster-targeting ruleset export.

nodes.label: Kasada
nodes.rationale: Classification-led analytics with drilldown and filtering; no evidence of a persistent operator entity. A LEAD, not evidence — Kasada's own site was not opened.

nodes.label: PayPal patent US12034731B2 — Evaluating access requests using assigned common actor identifiers
nodes.source_location: PRIOR ART — the most serious hit of the whole scan
nodes.author: PayPal
nodes.rationale: Filed 2021-01-29, granted 2024-07-09: the idea's mechanism as a granted patent — logs to groups to a stable per-actor id, persisted over a period such as the last 12 months. Differences: purpose is access-grant/fraud decisioning at login, not AI-crawler attribution; no operator-facing artifacts; nothing about JA4, HTTP/2 SETTINGS, header order or Web Bot Auth; and it is a patent, not something an operator can run. Consequence: drop any claim that nobody answers whether requests are one actor — someone patented answering it in 2021.

nodes.label: Patent US11652844B2 — Utilizing clustering to identify IP addresses used by a botnet
nodes.rationale: Surfaced but NOT OPENED — logged as a LEAD.

nodes.label: mshaheerjunaid/Panopticon
nodes.author: mshaheerjunaid
nodes.rationale: The only OSS project whose self-description IS this idea: 'clustering on behaviour and JA4 TLS fingerprint instead of IP'. MIT, Python, but 1 star, created and last pushed the same day, no community. FORK VERDICT: MECHANISM — a reference implementation to read and a naming collision to be aware of, weak as a fork base, and forking it is exactly the reskin trap.

nodes.label: Query-farm/vgi-tlsfp
nodes.author: Query-farm
nodes.rationale: PLUMBING and the best technical fit: JA3/JA3S/JA4 computed inside DuckDB with SQL, i.e. exactly the log-only single-binary SQL shape the product wants. MIT, Rust. Must ADD: log parser, the non-TLS join keys, swarm_id minting and cross-run persistence, the append-only ledger, the case card and the ruleset emitters.

nodes.label: CrowdSec
nodes.source_location: oss — CrowdSec, the flagged question answered
nodes.author: crowdsecurity
nodes.rationale: Not a clone and the single best plumbing fork base: nginx/Apache/Caddy parsers, acquisition and file tailer, GeoIP/AS enrichment, bouncers for enforcement. cscli decisions add takes --ip, --range or a custom scope you name, default scope 'Ip'; no documented construct mints a persistent identifier for a GROUP of distinct IPs recurring across days. A technically sharp judge will name CrowdSec and ask why swarm_id beats a decision — answer: CrowdSec's unit is an IP, Swarm Ledger's unit is a cluster that outlives every IP in it. Caveat: docs/scenarios/format/ fetched empty, so leaky-bucket groupby semantics should be confirmed before the pitch says CrowdSec cannot do this.

nodes.label: TecharoHQ/anubis
nodes.author: TecharoHQ
nodes.rationale: Proof-of-work gate, ~22,995 stars / 743 forks, created 2025-03-17 — a workaround, not attribution, and useful only as the 'what people do instead' baseline. For a planting/observation design it is actively harmful: it blocks the traffic you need to observe and destroys the record.

nodes.label: Logrip (arXiv:2508.03130) — Protecting Small Organizations from AI Bots with Hierarchical IP Hashing
nodes.author: Rama Carl Hoetzlein
nodes.rationale: Independently validates the segment ('small organizations, start ups, and self-hosted servers'), the gap ('distributed crawling attacks that conventional tools fail to identify') and the pain (80-95% of traffic from AI crawlers). But it aggregates by IP subnet hierarchy — precisely where the pitch claims to win, since an actor spread over 40 ASNs defeats subnet aggregation — and produces one-shot analysis plus visualisation with no stable id across runs, no TLS/HTTP-2/Web Bot Auth keys, and no ledger, case card or ruleset export. No dataset or code release mentioned.

nodes.label: arXiv:2606.30119 — Unmasking Web Agents with Multi-Layer Fingerprinting
nodes.author: Fayolle, Bouhenniche, Pelissier, Laperdrix, Maurice, Rudametkin
nodes.rationale: Network-, HTTP- and browser-level fingerprinting in honeysites against six LLM web agents — one-shot per-visit discrimination, no clustering of multiple IPs into one actor and no longitudinal identity. Honeypot data (1,383 visits, 2026-01-28 to 02-24) with no public release disclosed.

nodes.label: Zenodo 18895701 — Online Shop Server Logs for Bot Traffic (Dec 2025, anonymized)
nodes.rationale: Best available real dataset (CC BY 4.0, 178,939 requests, 28.6 MB) but stripped of exactly the keys the pitch leans on: 'IP addresses and User-Agent strings were replaced with stable pseudonyms'. STILL WORKS: path-sequence shingles, timing lockstep across distinct pseudonymous clients, co-occurrence clustering, swarm_id persistence across days (pseudonyms are stable). DEAD: ASN and /24 joins, JA4/TLS, HTTP/2 SETTINGS, header order, Web Bot Auth keyid — and the UA is pseudonymised so you cannot even print 'GPTBot'. Strongest demo = Zenodo base + the builder's own live log tail + a clearly labelled synthetic JA4-spoof scenario.

nodes.label: Grep-your-logs-for-AI-user-agents cottage industry
nodes.rationale: Strongest demo contrast available: the whole published state of the art for a non-CDN operator is 'grep for GPTBot|ClaudeBot|PerplexityBot' against a maintained user-agent list, which is defeated by one spoofed header. Seven live pages teaching the method were accessed 2026-10.

nodes.label: Comparative LLM methods for Social Media Bot Detection (Apart def/acc, 2nd place)
nodes.rationale: Closest past winner: social-media account classification with LLMs — no HTTP logs, no join keys, no cross-run operator identity, no operator artifacts. Shares only the words 'bot detection'.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: PLUMBING, fork freely (S4A)
nodes.rationale: vgi-tlsfp (JA4 in DuckDB) and CrowdSec (parsers, tailer, GeoIP/AS enrichment, bouncers) are pure upside; Anubis only as a positioning baseline. GoAccess, Matomo, Fail2ban, nepenthes, iocaine, go-away and the Nginx Bad Bot Blocker were not checked but are all presumed plumbing, since a GitHub query for bot-detection access-log clustering returned total_count 0.

nodes.label: Fork-base verdict: MECHANISM, do NOT fork (S4A)
nodes.rationale: Panopticon is the sole occupant: forking it means nothing is left to credit, because its one-line description already is the idea.
